lessons.title: The Anatomy of a Bubble: From Boom to Bust

body.text: Every bubble starts with a true story. It turns into a bubble the moment people stop buying the story and start buying the price.

markDefs.definition: A period in which the price of an asset rises far above any reasonable estimate of its underlying value, driven mainly by the expectation that prices will keep rising, and which eventually collapses.

children.text: Nobody wakes up and decides to join a bubble. A
bubble

feels, from the inside, like a sensible reaction to genuinely good news. That is what makes bubbles dangerous. If you can recognise the stages while you are living through one, you have a real edge over the crowd. This lesson gives you the map.
The Five Stages Every Bubble Goes Through

The economist Hyman Minsky described how credit booms turn into busts, and the historian Charles Kindleberger applied that framework to centuries of financial manias in his book Manias, Panics, and Crashes. Their five stage model fits Dutch tulips in the 1630s, the dot-com mania of the late 1990s and India's 2007 market with uncomfortable accuracy.

body.caption: The Kindleberger and Minsky Bubble Stages

cells: A genuine shock or innovation creates new profit opportunities
Early investors in the theme earn big, justified gains
Money flows in, often borrowed, and prices rise steadily
"The fundamentals are strong, earnings are growing"
Media coverage grows, new funds and IPOs launch on the theme
Prices detach from value, and caution is mocked
"This time is different", "prices can only go up"
First-time investors pile in, IPOs are hugely oversubscribed, valuations hit records
Insiders and smart money quietly sell, and the first sharp falls arrive
"It is just a healthy dip, buy more"
Falls get bigger, rallies get weaker, a big-name failure occurs
Everyone rushes for the exit at once, and prices overshoot below fair value
"Stocks are gambling, I am never investing again"
Good companies sell at bargain valuations, and nobody wants them

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The first stage of a bubble, when a real innovation or economic shift creates new profit opportunities, is called ___.
body.explanation: Displacement is the trigger, and it is usually grounded in something real: the internet in the 1990s, or India's high growth years after 2003. The bubble does not come from the displacement itself, but from what the crowd does with it in the stages that follow.

children.text: India's 2003 to 2008 Bubble, Stage by Stage
India's last great pre-2008 bull run is a near-perfect case study, because every stage shows up clearly in the data.

body.title: From Boom to Bust: Sensex and Nifty, 2003 to 2008

events.title: Displacement
events.description: Indian economic growth accelerates and corporate profits surge. The Nifty trades below 12 times earnings, cheap by historical standards. Early buyers are rewarded for backing a genuine story.

events.title: Boom
events.description: Foreign institutional investors pour money into India. The Sensex crosses 10,000 for the first time in February 2006. Infrastructure, real estate and capital goods become the market's favourite themes.

events.title: Euphoria
events.description: The Sensex doubles from 10,000 to cross 20,000 on 29 October 2007, in just 20 months. Realty and power stocks trade at extreme valuations and new IPOs are swamped with bids.

events.title: Distress
events.description: The Sensex hits its peak of 21,206.77 on 10 January and the Nifty PE crosses 28. Reliance Power's IPO draws record bids the next week. On 21 January the Sensex falls 1,408 points, its first ever four digit fall.

events.title: The Warning Shot
events.description: Reliance Power lists on 11 February and closes its first day 17% below its issue price. The most hyped IPO in Indian history loses money on day one.

events.title: Revulsion
events.description: Lehman Brothers collapses on 15 September and global panic spreads. The Sensex closes at 8,509.56 on 27 October, roughly 60% below its peak, and the Nifty PE falls to around 11.

stats.label: Nifty PE, 2003
stats.context: The starting point of the boom

stats.label: Nifty PE, late 2008
stats.context: Right back where the boom began

body.text: The India story of 2003 to 2008 was real. Nifty companies grew earnings at about 21% a year over the five years to 2008. The bubble was not in the story, it was in the price: investors paid 28 times earnings as if that growth could never slow. When it did, the PE multiple collapsed from 28 to 11, even though the companies still existed.

body.title: Which Stage Is This?
body.question: An IPO from a company with no operating history is oversubscribed more than 70 times. Your neighbour, who has never bought a share, borrows money to apply. Newspaper columns argue that old valuation rules no longer apply to India. Which stage does this describe?
body.explanation: First-time investors borrowing to chase an unproven company, record oversubscription and "the old rules no longer apply" are the three classic markers of euphoria. This describes India in January 2008, the week Reliance Power opened for bids, days after the Sensex hit its all-time high.

children.text: Reliance Power: A Bubble in a Single Stock

markDefs.definition: The belief that you can profit from buying an overpriced asset because someone else, a "greater fool", will buy it from you at an even higher price later.

children.text: Reliance Power's IPO opened on 15 January 2008, at the absolute peak of the bull market. The company had not yet generated power from its planned projects, but the brand name, the India growth story and a red hot primary market drew bids worth many times the shares on offer. Plenty of applicants were not investing in a power business at all. They were following the
greater fool theory
, expecting to sell to someone else on listing day.

stats.label: Oversubscription
stats.context: One of the most heavily bid IPOs in Indian history at the time

stats.label: Listing Day High
stats.context: About 19% above issue price, within minutes of listing

stats.label: Listing Day Close
stats.context: About 17% below issue price by the end of the session

children.text: The listing day swing tells the whole bubble story in six hours: euphoria at the open, distress by mid-morning, revulsion by the close. Investors who held on for the long run fared even worse. Ten years after listing, a ₹10,000 investment at the issue price was worth roughly ₹1,600.
The Valuation Stretch: Why Bubbles Need Impossible Growth

markDefs.definition: Price to Earnings ratio: the share price divided by earnings per share. A PE of 40 means investors are paying ₹40 for every ₹1 of annual profit the company earns.

children.text: The cleanest way to spot a bubble is to ask how long the business would need to grow to justify today's price. The
PE ratio
makes this easy. If a stock trades at 80 times earnings and the price does not move, earnings have to grow until the PE falls to a normal level.

body.caption: How many years of earnings growth it takes, at a flat share price, for a high PE to come down to a fair PE.
How Long Until a Stretched Valuation Looks Normal? (Fair PE assumed at 25, share price flat)

children.text: Read that table carefully. Even at a superb 20% earnings growth every single year, a stock at 80 times earnings needs over six years just to reach a PE of 25, and the shareholder earns nothing on price in the meantime. One bad year of growth, and the wait gets longer. In euphoria, investors quietly assume that nothing will go wrong for a decade.

body.title: Your Turn: The Waiting Game
body.prompt: A popular railway stock trades at a PE of 60. You believe a fair PE for the business is 20. If earnings grow 20% a year and the share price stays flat, how many years until the PE reaches 20? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Years = ln(60 ÷ 20) ÷ ln(1.20) = ln(3) ÷ ln(1.2) = 1.0986 ÷ 0.1823, which is about 6.0 years. Earnings must triple, and at 20% a year that takes six years of zero price return. If growth slows to 10%, it takes about 11.5 years. That is the hidden bet inside every stretched valuation.

body.title: A Genuine Boom vs a Bubble

columns.label: Genuine Boom
points: Prices rise roughly in line with earnings growth
Valuations are high but can be justified with realistic assumptions
Buyers talk about businesses, cash flows and competitive advantages
IPOs come from established, profitable companies
Leverage in the system stays moderate

columns.label: Bubble
points: Prices rise far faster than earnings, so PE multiples keep expanding
Valuations only work if everything goes right for a decade
Buyers talk about the price, listing gains and what others are making
IPOs come from young, unproven or loss making companies, and are still oversubscribed many times over
Borrowing to buy shares becomes common among ordinary investors

children.text: Modern Froth: The SME IPO Frenzy

Bubbles do not only happen in giant indices. They also form in small corners of the market. In August 2024, Resourceful Automobile, a Delhi dealer selling Yamaha two-wheelers from two showrooms with 8 permanent employees, raised ₹12 crore through an IPO on the BSE SME platform at ₹117 a share. The issue was subscribed about 419 times, with bids worth close to ₹4,800 crore.

body.label: Resourceful Automobile SME IPO, August 2024
body.value: About 400 rupees bid for every rupee on offer
body.context: A ₹12 crore issue attracted bids worth close to ₹4,800 crore, for a business with two showrooms. The frenzy was about expected listing gains, not the business.

body.text: SEBI responded to the SME IPO frenzy by tightening the rules in March 2025. SME issuers now need an operating profit (EBITDA) of at least ₹1 crore in two of the last three financial years, and the offer for sale portion is capped at 20% of the issue size. Rules like these reduce the worst excesses, but no regulation can stop a crowd from overpaying.

body.title: Bubble Warning Signs: Check Any Hot Theme
steps: Pick a sector or stock that everyone around you is talking about right now
Look up its PE on Screener.in and compare it with its own 5 year and 10 year median PE
Check whether profits have grown as fast as the share price over the last 3 years
Count how many IPOs or new fund offers have launched on this theme in the last 12 months
Notice whether people discuss the business or only the price and recent returns
Ask: what would earnings growth need to be for the next 10 years to justify today's price?
Write down which of the five bubble stages you think this theme is in, and why

body.title: The Cousin and the Grey Market Premium
body.scenario: Your cousin messages you excitedly. An SME IPO opening tomorrow is already subscribed 180 times on day one, and a Telegram channel says the grey market premium is 90%. The company was incorporated four years ago, and the IPO document shows most of its revenue comes from a single customer. Your cousin plans to take a ₹2 lakh personal loan to apply in several family members' names to improve the odds of allotment.
body.prompt: Which bubble stage do these signals point to, what are the specific risks, and what would you tell your cousin?
body.modelAnswer: These are euphoria signals: extreme oversubscription, a grey market premium driving demand, unofficial tips on Telegram, and an ordinary investor borrowing to chase listing gains. The specific risks are several. First, the grey market is unofficial and unregulated, so its premium is not a promise of anything. Second, dependence on a single customer is a concentration risk that nobody in the frenzy is pricing in. Third, SME shares trade in large lots with thin volumes, so selling after listing can be difficult if sentiment turns. Fourth, borrowing to buy turns a possible loss into a certain debt: the loan and interest must be repaid whatever the share does. Applying in family members' names with borrowed money also creates friction and potential disputes within the family. You should not tell your cousin what to buy or sell, but you can point out that the demand is being driven by expected listing gains rather than the business, and that borrowing to chase a price is the single most reliable way a bubble turns into personal financial damage. At minimum, read the offer document on BSE or NSE rather than a Telegram channel.

body.title: A Caveat Before You Compare Nifty PE Across the Years

children.text: From 1 April 2021, NSE began calculating the Nifty 50 PE using consolidated earnings instead of standalone earnings. Consolidated earnings include subsidiaries, so they are usually higher, which makes the reported PE lower than it would have been under the old method.
The practical impact:
a Nifty PE of 22 today is not directly comparable with a PE of 22 in 2008 or 2020.
What to do:
compare valuations within the same method period, or use a second measure such as price to book or market capitalisation to GDP alongside PE.
Bubble spotting depends on comparisons with history, so always check that the history is measured the same way.

body.label: Nifty Indices: Historical PE, PB and Dividend Yield
body.description: Download the Nifty 50's historical PE ratio. Find the readings for January 2008, March 2020 and today, and ask which bubble stage the numbers suggest.

cards.definition: A period when an asset's price rises far above its underlying value, driven mainly by expectations of further price rises, before collapsing.
The first stage of a bubble: a genuine innovation or shock that creates new profit opportunities.
The stage where prices detach from value, caution is mocked, and first-time investors pile in believing prices can only rise.
The final panic stage, when everyone sells at once and prices overshoot below fair value.
Buying an overpriced asset in the belief that someone else will pay even more for it later.
Share price divided by earnings per share. It shows how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of annual profit.

points: Bubbles follow five recognisable stages: displacement, boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion
Every bubble begins with a real story; the bubble lies in the price investors pay for that story, not in the story itself
India's 2003 to 2008 run saw the Nifty PE expand from below 12 to about 28, then collapse back to about 11 by late 2008
Reliance Power's IPO, oversubscribed over 70 times and closing 17% below issue price on listing day, was euphoria and distress in a single stock
The valuation stretch test asks how many years of growth a price already assumes; at PE 80 and 20% growth, reaching PE 25 takes over six years of flat returns
Extreme oversubscription, borrowing to buy and "this time is different" talk are the loudest euphoria signals, as the 2024 SME IPO frenzy showed
